```{r, setup, include=FALSE}
library(sloop)
```

## Introduction

Over the past six months, I have been assisting a public health agency as a 
reporting analyst. 
We face significant challenges in managing and interpreting diverse and 
voluminous vaccine data such as MMR, influenza, and COVID-19. 
Each vaccine type presents unique data characteristics, creating a multifaceted 
information landscape.

We have developed our own R package to help simplify vaccine data analysis. 
It reduces repetitive coding and introduces a standardised approach to the 
complexities inherent in vaccine data.

In this post, I explore the potential of integrating S3 classes into our data 
analysis toolkit. 
For the most part, I view object-oriented programming as an added complexity for
my day-to-day work, and even for my packages. 
However, the unique challenges posed by vaccine data have provided me with a 
good opportunity to potentially utilise OOP, and I wanted to highlight the 
benefits of S3 classes in simplifying complex data analysis.

## Polymorphism: The Many Shapes of Vaccination Data

Our work often revolves around the 'vaccine events' table, seemingly simple but 
complex upon deeper analysis. 
Categorising individuals by vaccination status becomes intricate with the varied
schedules of different vaccines. 
We also adapt our analysis to various demographic or geographic segments, 
underscoring the need for a versatile approach.

Here, S3 classes in R offer a solution. 
Their flexibility and simplicity can standardise our process while accommodating
each vaccine's unique characteristics. 
This is where the concept of polymorphism, or 'many shapes', in Object-Oriented 
Programming (OOP) becomes vital. 
Polymorphism allows functions like `summary()` in R to adapt their behaviour 
based on the data type:

```{r, summary-example}
diamonds <- ggplot2::diamonds

summary(diamonds$carat)
summary(diamonds$cut)
```

In this example, `summary()` varies its output based on whether it's summarising
numerical data (carat) or categorical data (cut). 
Such polymorphic functions in our vaccine data analysis would enable handling 
diverse data types efficiently, aligning with the varied nature of our data and 
enhancing workflow efficiency.

## S3 Classes in R: An Overview and Demonstration

Unlike Python's singular OOP system, R offers three systems: S3, S4, and R6. 
S3's flexibility and minimalistic design, as highlighted in Hadley Wickham's 
[Advanced R](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/s3.html), provides significant programming 
freedom. 
This is especially useful for managing diverse datasets like vaccine data.

Let's start by defining a constructor for vaccine data. 
A constructor in R is a function that creates and initialises an S3 object:

```{r, define-constructor}
# Constructor for vaccine data
new_vaccine_data <- function(data, vaccine_type) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data))  # Ensure data is a dataframe
  stopifnot(is.character(vaccine_type) && length(vaccine_type) == 1)  # Validate vaccine_type
  
  structure(data, class = c(vaccine_type, "vaccine_data", "data.frame"))
}

# Create mock data frame
vaccine_df <- data.frame(patient_id = 1:10, vaccine_date = Sys.Date())

# Apply 'constructor' class to dataframe
mmr_vaccine_data <- new_vaccine_data(vaccine_df, "mmr")
covid_vaccine_data <- new_vaccine_data(vaccine_df, "covid")

# Print the 'class' of the object.
class(mmr_vaccine_data)
```

This constructor simplifies the process of tagging dataframes with specific 
vaccine types.

Next, a custom print method demonstrates how S3 class attributes can be used:

```{r, print-demo}
# Custom print method for vaccine data
print.vaccine_data <- function(x, ...) {
  vaccine_type <- attr(x, "class")[1]
  cat("Vaccine Type:", vaccine_type, "\n")
  NextMethod()
}

print(mmr_vaccine_data)
```

After defining our custom print method, it's important to understand the role of
`NextMethod()` in this context. 
In S3 classes, `NextMethod()` is used to call the next method in the hierarchy. 
[
The *hierarchy* referred to by `NextMethod()` is determined by the class 
attribute of the object. 
The class attribute is a character vector where each element represents a 
different class which you can check with `class(obj)`. 
The order of these classes in the vector dictates the method hierarchy. 
When `NextMethod()` is called, it looks for the next method to execute based on 
this class hierarchy. 
If the first element in the class attribute doesn't have a specific method, 
`NextMethod()` will search for a method corresponding to the next element in the
class attribute, and so on. 
This mechanism allows for a form of inheritance where methods from more general 
classes can be used if more specific methods aren't available.
]{.aside} In our `print.vaccine_data` function, after printing the vaccine type,
`NextMethod()` ensures that the standard data frame print method is also 
executed. 
This combination allows for custom behavior (displaying the vaccine type) while 
maintaining the default data frame print behavior, demonstrating the 
adaptability of S3 methods.

In any case, this custom print method defined above, showcases the practicality 
and simplicity of using S3 classes in R. 
By customising the print function, we can make it easier for our analysts to 
track what datasets are being used.

Now it's worth considering how we could further leverage our S3 classes with 
specific methods tailored for different vaccines. 
For instance, we could develop a `add_vax_status()` function with unique methods
like `add_vax_status.mmr()` and `add_vax_status.covid()`. 
Each method could handle vaccine-specific criteria for determining vaccination 
status, reflecting the unique schedules and requirements of each vaccine type. 
Incorporating these methods into our S3 framework would significantly enhance 
our ability to process and interpret vaccine data with precision and 
context-specific insights.

Let's introduce a practical application of S3 classes with the `add_vax_status()` 
function. 
This function demonstrates polymorphism by adapting its behavior based on the 
vaccine type. 
For instance:

```{r, demonstrate-add-vax-status}
add_vax_status <- function(data) {
  UseMethod("add_vax_status")
}

add_vax_status.covid <- function(data) {
  cat("Adding COVID vax status\n")
  # Specific logic for COVID vaccine
}

add_vax_status.mmr <- function(data) {
  cat("Adding MMR vax status\n")
  # Specific logic for MMR vaccine
}
```

Now let's try for MMR:

```{r, add-vax-status-mmr}
add_vax_status(mmr_vaccine_data)
```

and Covid:

```{r, add-vax-status-covid}
add_vax_status(covid_vaccine_data)
```

As shown, when invoked with a dataset, `add_vax_status` identifies the vaccine 
type (COVID or MMR) and executes the corresponding method. 
This not only simplifies the code but ensures that each vaccine type is handled 
appropriately, showcasing the power of polymorphism in streamlining our data 
analysis tasks.

## Conclusion

This exploration of S3 classes in R demonstrates their potential in streamlining
vaccine data analysis. 
The adaptability and simplicity of S3 classes offer a promising solution to the 
complexities we face. 
As we continue to develop our R package, the integration of these 
object-oriented principles could greatly enhance our analytic capabilities, 
ultimately benefiting public health decision-making. 
Rest assured, I will keep you posted on what we end up doing, and it's 
effectiveness.
